@sbomer could you have a look please?

We're already in this situation with ILLink so this doesn't really make the problem worse - but I have a slight concern about how easy it is for developers to reason about these optimizations.

The optimization can influence the trim warnings from ILC, so to provide a consistent UX the analyzer would need to support the same optimizations, which might not be possible when the constant method is defined in a ref assembly. Curious if you have any thoughts on the long term direction of this kind of optimization and the analyzer behavior.

> We're already in this situation with ILLink so this doesn't really make the problem worse - but I have a slight concern about how easy it is for developers to reason about these optimizations.

I don't look at these as something to reason about - if there's a trim safety issue and things are not properly annotated with feature guards/etc., the warning from the analyzer is correct.

If whole program analysis/inlining/whatever makes it that the problematic code is no longer there, I look at that as a bonus, not something to rely on. The problem is really only when one needs this to be reliable, but then they need to property annotate the API so that the fact that the API can be substituted is contractual (e.g. with a feature guard attribute). Without the contract, it's just a bonus. An analyzer should still flag such uses as problematic.

issue_context.title: ilc doesn't trim some code referenced only from trimmed methods
issue_context.body:
### Description

In some cases, `ilc` keeps some code in the final executable, but the only code path accessing it has been trimmed.

### Reproduction Steps

Clone https://github.com/MrJul/repro-ilc-not-trimming
Run `dotnet publish -r win-x64`

This is a very stripped down version of code from Avalonia reproducing the problem.
(Note that in this example, only one type is kept, but in Avalonia there are more.)

### Expected behavior

Everything in LinuxLib is trimmed, only WindowsLib is referenced.

### Actual behavior

`X11RenderingMode` from LinuxLib isn't trimmed, but all methods using it have been removed.

In the following screenshots, we can notice that `X11RenderingMode` is referenced from `X11PlatformOptions`'s constructor, which has been trimmed away:
![sizoscope types](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0cfdb3da-8604-4f4a-ac38-6766f478bc9c)
![sizoscope paths](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/65bac5c1-ea55-4f4d-b6d6-bd01ad7c03e2)


### Regression?

No.

### Known Workarounds

_No response_

### Configuration

Latest `Microsoft.DotNet.ILCompiler` from daily build, 9.0.0-rc.1.24381.5

### Other information

For comparison, `ILLink` works fine in this scenario: no `LinuxLib` assembly is visible in the trimmed folder.

Note that with .NET 8.0.7, the whole call path (`X11PlatformOptions`, `AvaloniaX11PlatformExtensions`, etc.) is incorrectly kept by `ilc`.

With .NET 9.0.0-rc.1.24381.5, only `X11RenderingMode` is kept. I couldn't find the PR that fixed the above, but it's probably related to this issue.

The compiler has two phases: scanning phase that figures out what is reachable, including reachable from reflection, and a compilation phase that does actual codegen. Compilation phase could get rid of this (through inlining and dead code elimination), but the scanning phase didn't (scanning phase doesn't inline). The damage to whole program view couldn't be undone. We might be able to do limited inlining for this case.

(The reason this was generated was reflection analysis - Sizoscope just doesn't show that. Rename the *.codegen.dgml file to *.scan.dgml (replacing the original scan.dgml in the obj directory) and reopen the mstat in sizoscope - it will show the type was kept due to reflection.)

Thank you for your answer and the tip to rename the dgml file, it helps better understanding the root causes!

----

I realize my stripped down example was maybe a bit too simple.
In this specific case, I assume the reflection usage is because ilc thinks it's needed for the underlying array type? (Even though it should still be trimmed.)

In a real Avalonia app, `UsePlatformDetect()` keeps a lot of other types unrelated to reflection - for example unused implementations of used interfaces.

My main concern here is that ILLink is able to figure out that all of these types are unreachable and must completely removed. I would naively expect ILC to have similar capabilities. (In fact I've used `PublishTrimmed` without `PublishAot` several times in the past to ensure that conditionally unreferenced code is properly trimmed before publishing with AOT, as it's faster to have a look at trimmed assemblies with various decompilers. But that was a bad assumption.)

Don't worry, I understand that it's not at easy as sharing some code between the two applications :)

> In this specific case, I assume the reflection usage is because ilc thinks it's needed for the underlying array type? (Even though it should still be trimmed.)

Specifically for enum types, the compiler has an assumption that if the type was touched in a significant way, it was reflected on. Making an array of the enum is "significant".

The general problem is that we didn't "inline" the OS detection API calls even though they return constant true/false and looked at the (eventually) dead branch while building the whole program view. The fix is not to look at this dead branch. ILLink does that, ILC doesn't (right now). This is in a similar bucket as https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/88796#issuecomment-1635216001. Would be nice to fix. I guess this issue will finally force me to look into it.

review_comments: Does there need to be any special handling for intrinsics that fold to a constant (like `Vector128.IsHardwareAccelerated` or `Sse.IsSupported`)?

I expect those to be trivially rejected since this rejects any methods marked intrinsic:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/f8b5e181f1bbe90f2c5a8420b7aaf60522327229/src/coreclr/tools/aot/ILCompiler.Compiler/Compiler/SubstitutedILProvider.cs#L667-L673

So in that case, helper properties that themselves are just returning constant instrinsics won't be substituted still, right? Is that something we want to support in the future?

In the libraries, we have some properties like:
```csharp
public static bool Vectorizable => (typeof(T) == typeof(double)) || (typeof(T) == typeof(float));
```

and other libraries like `ImageSharp` have APIs like:
```csharp
public static bool IsSupported => AdvSimd.IsSupported;

public sealed override bool IsAvailable => IsSupported;
```

So this comes to mind as something that would be nice to ensure the right substitutions are also happening

Yeah, once RyuJIT does the scanning, the scanned view of the program can be much better. RyuJIT already does this substitution when doing codegen; this PR just tries to approximate what RyuJIT will do a bit more so that we avoid some of the damage to whole program view (80-20 principle).
👍 Thanks for answering, was mostly just interested in the planned direction here; sounds great!

I'm curious which assert was hit. It seems linker's CompilerGeneratedState sees the IL after it's processed by UnreachableBlocksOptimizer, so I'm wondering why this needs to be different (but don't see a problem with it either).

I wanted to point you to the build but looks like AzDo did the thing again where build results are gone in less than 3 days for whatever reason: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/runs/28413388145

I'll submit a PR with the subset of commits that hit this so we can see the assert again.

This is handling direct constants. Are indirect constants also desirable to be handled or are they possible handled elsewhere?

Consider something like `public static float X => DegreesToRadians(90);`, where the `DegreesToRadians(90)` call can be trivially folded and so `X` is effectively producing a constant

I considered just hooking this into the cctor interpreter, but I don't know if I want to go there. This runs on all IL and if it gets too fancy, we might see it on throughput.

We should ideally not have to do this rewriting - we should use RyuJIT as the IL scanner because RyuJIT already can do this (and more) better.
